opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really interesting question, and honestly one I think about a lot, because most of the work on norm learning focuses on the acquisition side. How do you pick up a norm from observing people? Much less attention goes to how norms get revised or abandoned. But that's clearly a huge part of how human normative systems actually work.

In the kind of framework I've been working with, you treat norms as latent structure that an agent infers from behavior. You observe people acting, and you ask what shared rules or constraints would best explain why they're doing what they're doing, beyond just their individual goals. Within that Bayesian setup, unlearning a norm isn't a separate mechanism bolted on. It falls out of the same inference process. If you keep observing behavior that's inconsistent with a norm you previously believed was in force, your posterior on that norm should drop. Maybe people are no longer complying, or violations no longer get sanctioned, or the people you thought were following the rule were really just acting on their own preferences.

There are some subtleties, though, that make it more interesting than updating a probability downward.

The first is distinguishing a norm that no longer exists from a norm that still exists but is being violated. Humans are pretty good at this. If I see someone run a red light, I don't conclude traffic laws have been abolished. So the model needs some representation of compliance as imperfect, and of what counts as evidence the norm itself has lapsed. That evidence includes things like the absence of sanctioning, the absence of disapproval, or widespread and open non-compliance rather than isolated deviations.

The second is non-stationarity. Norms change over time, so you don't want an agent that assumes the set of norms is fixed forever and just gets more and more confident. You want a model where norms can come into and go out of existence, something like a change-point or dynamic model over the normative structure. Then recent evidence can carry more weight, and the agent can recognize when something has shifted rather than treating new behavior as noise.

The third, which connects to a lot of what I care about philosophically, is that norms aren't just statistical regularities. They often have a function or a rationale. Part of what lets people let go of a norm is realizing it no longer serves the purpose it was meant to serve, or that it was never justified to begin with. So a richer version of the framework would let agents reason about why a norm exists. It might solve a coordination problem, or reflect something people would mutually agree to. Then when circumstances change so that rationale no longer holds, the agent has grounds to revise the norm even before it sees everyone else abandoning it.

That last piece matters a lot for AI alignment. You don't want systems that are purely conformist, absorbing whatever norms happen to be prevalent and only updating when the crowd moves. You also don't want systems that unilaterally decide norms don't apply to them. So the interesting design space is in between: agents that track what norms are actually in force in a community, understand the reasons behind them, and can participate in the process of norm revision in a way that's legitimate and accountable, rather than just drifting or defecting.

r001.rationale: The response describes inferring latent norms from observed behavior and updating beliefs Bayesianly, but does not propose identifying an underlying generative model over which that inference produces norm-based behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I think about a lot, because in the framework I've been developing, norms aren't really stored as fixed rules in the agent's head. They're inferred. The agent is doing something like Bayesian inference over what the norms in a given community are, based on observing behavior, observing sanctions, observing what people say when someone violates an expectation. So in that picture, "unlearning" isn't a separate operation you bolt on afterwards. It's just what happens when the evidence changes.

Let me make that concrete. If I'm an agent and I've built up a posterior that, say, this group has a norm against interrupting, and then I start seeing people interrupt freely and nobody reacts, nobody sanctions it, nobody even seems to notice, that's evidence. My posterior should shift. The norm either never existed in the way I thought, or it's eroded, or there's some contextual exception I didn't understand. And the nice thing about treating norms as inferred latent variables rather than as a hard-coded ruleset is that this updating is principled. You don't have to decide in advance which norms are revisable. All of them are, in proportion to how much evidence you had for them in the first place.

Now, where it gets harder, and where I think the interesting research questions are, is that norms aren't just beliefs about what people do. They have this normative force. People actually care about them, and they expect others to care. So if a norm is changing in a community, there's a transitional period where some people still hold the old norm and some people don't, and an agent has to track that heterogeneity. You can't just collapse to "the norm is gone." You have to represent something like, the norm is contested, or the norm applies in these subgroups but not those ones.

The other thing I'd say is that in a lot of the work people do on AI alignment, norms get smuggled in as if they were preferences, like reward functions, and then unlearning becomes this awkward process of fine-tuning the model away from a behavior. I think that's kind of the wrong level of description. Norms are social facts. They're facts about what a group expects and will enforce. And so the right way to unlearn one is to let the agent see that the group's expectations have shifted, not to surgically remove some weight pattern. If you do it the surgical way, you lose the thing that makes norm-following generalize, which is the understanding of why the norm was there and who it was for.

So the short answer is: I'd treat it as inference, make sure the model is representing uncertainty and heterogeneity over norms rather than point estimates, and then unlearning falls out of ordinary belief revision rather than needing a special mechanism. The hard part is making sure the agent is actually paying attention to the right evidence, especially the absence of sanctions, which is easy to miss.

r001.rationale: The response describes norms as latent variables inferred through Bayesian reasoning from behavior, sanctions, and statements, rather than as fixed rules. That communicates the proposed generative account behind norm-based behavior.

astra-6.text:
I would start by distinguishing two things: unlearning the belief that a norm is in force, and changing whether you think that norm ought to be followed. Those are different kinds of updates. You can recognize that a community expects a certain behavior while also deciding that the expectation is unjustified.

Within the framework, I’d try to represent norms as things that can be inferred and revised, rather than as fixed constraints. Then the question becomes: what evidence would lead you to revise a norm? Perhaps the circumstances that justified it no longer hold. Perhaps you discover that it conflicts with a more important value, or that the people affected by it have good reasons to reject it.

The tricky part is that observing people violate a norm doesn’t, by itself, tell you that you should abandon it. So I think unlearning has to involve reasoning about the justification for the norm, not just tracking how often people comply. Ideally, you’d revise the particular expectation while preserving whatever underlying concern still makes sense.

r001.rationale: The response discusses revising norms based on evidence and justification, but does not propose identifying an underlying generative model or describe Bayesian inference producing norm-based behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’d distinguish between unlearning a norm and unlearning the tendency to treat that norm as authoritative. You might still need to understand a norm to predict how other people will behave, even if you no longer think you should follow it.

So, in this framework, I’d want norms to be represented as things you can reason about and revise, rather than simply being baked into a policy. You could ask: What evidence led me to infer this norm? Who endorses it? What purpose does it serve, and does it actually serve that purpose? If those assumptions change, then your commitment to the norm should be able to change as well.

The harder case is when the norm shapes what you even consider as an alternative. Then merely receiving contradictory evidence might not be enough. You need some way of exploring other possible ways of acting, or encountering people who organize their lives differently. So I think unlearning would involve both revising your beliefs and expanding the space of possibilities you’re able to consider.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making norms explicit, revising beliefs, and exploring alternatives, but does not identify an underlying generative model or Bayesian inference as the basis of norm-based behavior.
